task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of August 10, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style newspaper news update on changes at the Vesper Quay grain terminal and what its smaller order book means for workers and nearby growers.

facts.text: Vesper Quay Grain Terminal announced Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, that it will stop routine Sunday loading in October.
The terminal has signed autumn export orders for 180,000 tons, compared with 240,000 tons at the same point last year.
The 60,000-ton difference is a 25% decline in booked volume, not a measure of all grain produced in the region.
Pelden Grain Trading, which had booked 40,000 tons at the same point last year, canceled its planned 40,000-ton order for this autumn after changing storage arrangements.
That lost customer order accounts for 40,000 tons of the 60,000-ton year-to-year decline; the terminal has not explained the remaining 20,000 tons.
The new seasonal-staff roster allocates 4,800 paid hours, compared with 6,000 in last autumn's roster, a 20% reduction; actual hours worked and each employee's allocation are not supplied.
Nineteen permanent jobs will remain, but 12 seasonal employees will receive shorter contracts.
The hours reduction is smaller than the volume reduction because inspection and maintenance work will continue, according to operations director Mara Keld.
The terminal's weekday truck-receiving hours will remain unchanged.
Growers with existing delivery contracts may still deliver the contracted quantities; the terminal has not announced a new farmgate price.
Seasonal loader Evin Moss also works at a winter warehouse but does not start that job until November.
Moss said, "A shorter season leaves a space in the calendar that the next job does not automatically fill."
The terminal has offered affected seasonal staff first consideration for unscheduled vessel work, without guaranteeing additional hours.
Grower association chair Lora Flint said some members can store grain themselves while others depend on prompt delivery slots.
Keld said, "We are matching the loading roster to signed ships, not predicting the size of the harvest."
The terminal handles grain from 63 contracted farms and also stores grain for two food manufacturers.
Its storage business is covered by separate contracts and is not included in the 180,000-ton export figure.
The port authority said it has not changed the terminal's berth allocation or handling charges.
The terminal's oldest silo dates to 1981; a newer covered conveyor opened in 2018.
No regional harvest estimate or evidence connecting this order decline to a wider trade policy is included in the reporting record.
